records.why: The wheelbarrow supporting phenomenon was backwards. With the wheel axle as pivot, the load W at distance a from the axle and the lifting force F at the handles at distance L, balance gives F x L = W x a, so F = W x a / L. A smaller a (load nearer the wheel) needs a smaller F, so it is EASIER to lift. Check with numbers: a 600 N load at 0.4 m from the axle and handles at 1.2 m need F = 600 x 0.4 / 1.2 = 200 N; the same load at 0.8 m needs 400 N.

records.new: Learners notice that placing the load close to the wheel (the pivot) is much easier to lift than placing it further back towards the handles, because a shorter distance from the pivot gives the load a smaller moment.
records.reference: OpenStax College Physics 2e, Chapter 9 'Statics and Torque' (torque, static equilibrium, simple machines)

records.value: The jembe is NOT a couple: one effort force at the grip acts at a distance d from the blade pivot, so its moment is M = F × d and a longer handle gives a larger moment (Lessons 2 and 3). A couple needs two equal and opposite forces, as with two hands on a steering wheel: spreading the hands apart increases the distance d between the forces, so the same push from each hand gives a larger turning effect. Both ideas use the rule moment = force × distance, but the distance is measured differently: from the pivot to the force for a single force, and between the two forces for a couple.

records.new: uses a 2.4 m wooden oar as a lever to row his boat. The oar turns about the rowlock (the pivot), which is 0.4 m from the blade end. He pulls with a force of 80 N at the handle end, and the water pushes back on the blade end with a force of 480 N. (a) Identify the effort, load, and pivot. (b) Calculate the moment of Ochieng's effort about the pivot. (c) Calculate the moment of the water force about the pivot. Is the oar in equilibrium? Show your working.

records.why: No answer key was given for the marked paper. Recomputed: 2.4 - 0.4 = 2.0; 80 x 2.0 = 160; 480 x 0.4 = 192. 3 x 30 = 90; 90 / 4 = 22.5 cm, and 50 + 22.5 = 72.5 cm (on the other side of the pivot). 200 x 1.8 = 360. 50 x 0.4 = 20; 50 x 0.8 = 40.
records.old: Collect all papers promptly.
records.new: Collect all papers promptly. ANSWER KEY — Item 1: effort = the 80 N pull at the handle, load = the 480 N water force on the blade, pivot = the rowlock; effort moment 80 × 2.0 = 160 N·m; load moment 480 × 0.4 = 192 N·m; not in equilibrium (160 < 192). Item 2: 3 N × 30 cm = 90 N·cm = 4 N × d, so d = 22.5 cm, at the 72.5 cm mark. Item 3: (a) 0 N; (b) 200 N × 1.8 m = 360 N·m; (c) it rotates but does not translate (zero resultant force, non-zero moment). Item 4: (a) 50 × 0.4 = 20 N·m and 50 × 0.8 = 40 N·m; (b) the longer handle doubles the distance from the pivot, so the moment doubles for the same force.

records.why: As written, the teacher called learners one at a time to ONE bench for 15 minutes; with 40 learners that is under 40 seconds each for three questions with 10-second waits, and the teacher notes themselves contradicted it (8 stations prepared, 'two simultaneous stations' for 40 learners). Groups of 4-5 at 8 stations with 2 minutes per group fits 15 minutes (8 x 2 = 16, about 15 with rounding) and still gives every learner an individual question. The teacher must decide whether to assess in groups like this or to assess the practical over several lessons.
records.old: PART A — PRACTICAL ASSESSMENT (15 minutes, staggered): While most of the class completes a structured peer-review task (see below), the teacher calls learners one at a time to the demonstration bench. Each learner is given a metre rule balanced on a pencil pivot at the 50 cm mark, two known masses (e.g., a 100 g stone tied with string at a known position), and a third unknown mass. The learner must: (i) hang the two known masses at specified positions, (ii) find the position to hang the third mass to achieve balance, and (iii) verbally explain what they did using the Principle of Moments ('The sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anti-clockwise moments'). Teacher awards marks for correct placement AND for verbal explanation. While waiting, learners complete a peer-review of a model answer to Item 2 (printed on a card), marking it using a provided 3-point rubric.
records.new: PART A — PRACTICAL ASSESSMENT (15 minutes, by group): Learners work in groups of four or five at practical stations while the teacher visits each station in turn (about 2 minutes per group). Each station has a metre rule balanced on a pencil pivot at the 50 cm mark, two known masses (e.g., a 100 g stone tied with string at a known position), and a third unknown mass. The group must: (i) hang the two known masses at specified positions, (ii) find the position to hang the third mass to achieve balance, and (iii) explain what they did using the Principle of Moments ('The sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anti-clockwise moments'). When the teacher arrives, each member answers one of the three questions (the teacher chooses who, and rotates the questions between groups), so every learner is assessed on at least one question; marks are given for correct placement AND for the verbal explanation. Before the teacher arrives, and while the teacher is at another station, learners complete a peer-review of a model answer to Item 2 (printed on a card), marking it using a provided 3-point rubric.

records.why: The rubric descriptors now name the levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches Expectations) so teachers can see the CBE level wording in the printed text. The couples criterion also now asks for a calculation, matching the new Part 4(f). The old text did not change otherwise.

value.criterion: Use of M = F × d and the Principle of Moments
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: calculates every moment correctly with units, converts masses to weights using g = 10 N/kg, identifies clockwise and anticlockwise moments, and states the Principle of Moments accurately.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: calculates most moments correctly with units and states the Principle of Moments with minor gaps, such as a missing direction or unit.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: makes frequent calculation errors, omits units or directions, or cannot state the Principle of Moments.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: identifies the blade-soil contact as the pivot and explains that the longer handle (90 cm against 30 cm) gives a larger perpendicular distance and so a larger moment for the same force, rejecting the idea that a bigger force is needed.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: explains that a longer handle makes digging easier and refers to distance and moment, but the pivot or the same-force reasoning is incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: says only that a longer handle is easier or gives vague reasons, without linking to moment, pivot or perpendicular distance.

value.criterion: Understanding of couples and net moment
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: defines a couple correctly, explains zero net force with pure rotation, calculates the moment of a couple using F × d with the distance between the forces, and explains a real couple such as the two-handed steering wheel grip. Uses the perpendicular distance, not the arrow length.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: defines a couple and gives F × d, with small gaps in the calculation, in explaining net force, or in the steering wheel example.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: confuses a couple with a single force, or does not explain why the object turns.

value.criterion: Connecting to Kenyan contexts and the driving question
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: gives a coherent answer to the driving question with at least two correct Kenyan examples, each with pivot and design reason, and clearly shows how thinking changed since Lesson 1.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: gives a mostly complete answer with two examples, where the pivot or design reasoning is partly missing.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: gives one example or none, with little link to the driving question or to the change in thinking.
